payload.rationale: The question resolves YES only if the seasonally adjusted headline CPI monthly change for October 2026, as published at one decimal on November 10, 2026, prints 0.5% or higher. Observed 2026 monthly headline prints (Feb 0.3, Mar 0.9, Apr 0.6, May 0.5, Jun -0.4, Jul 0.1, Aug 0.4) show an unusually volatile, energy-driven inflation year; 3 of 7 observed months met the >0.4% bar. August core was 0.3% and gasoline +3.9%, with 12-month headline at 3.4%, and September FOMC projections put 2026 PCE inflation at 3.7% and core PCE at 3.4%, confirming an elevated-inflation regime. In such regimes, historically roughly 20-35% of monthly prints reach 0.5%, versus well under 10% in normal times. A print of 0.5%+ typically requires core near 0.3-0.4% plus another meaningful energy increase, or a core spike. With core running ~0.3% and no information on September/October energy prices, my central expectation is a headline print in the 0.2-0.4% range, with a fat upper tail. Too high risk: the June-August pattern (-0.4, 0.1, 0.4) may reflect an energy shock unwinding, and if gasoline flattens or falls in October, a 0.5%+ print becomes unlikely (probability could be nearer 10-15%). Too low risk: this year has already produced three 0.5%+ months, FOMC projections imply inflation staying well above target through year-end, and any renewed energy or tariff pass-through surge in October could easily push headline to 0.5-0.6%, so 30%+ is plausible. I settle near 0.22.
limitations: No September or October price data, gasoline futures, or forecaster consensus for October CPI are supplied.
Rounding at one decimal makes the 0.4 vs 0.5 boundary sensitive to small component moves.
PCE annual projections are only a loose proxy for monthly CPI dynamics.
Estimate relies on historical regime base rates rather than a fitted component model.
